title: The unborn
hook: Bankei taught ordinary people: you already have the unborn Buddha-mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bassui's question: when a sound comes, who is hearing? Your line: stay with the not-finding.

A man comes to a Zen teacher with a confession. I was born with a short temper, he says. It's just how I am. How do I fix it? The teacher looks interested. That's remarkable, he says. Show it to me. The man says he can't, not right now; it only comes out when something sets it off. Then, says the teacher, it isn't something you were born with. You make it, on the spot. The teacher was Bankei, and he told plain stories like this to ordinary people.
screen: `I WAS BORN THIS WAY.` → `SHOW IT TO ME.` → `YOU MAKE IT ON THE SPOT.`

segments.voice: Bankei was a Japanese Rinzai Zen teacher whose teaching fits in a sentence: everyone already has the Buddha-mind, and it is unborn. First, unborn. Bankei means a mind never produced, never put together, so it can never fall apart. It's here before you start building moods and grudges and stories, and it handles everything perfectly well without your adding anything. Second, ordinary people. Bankei spoke everyday Japanese, not the scholar's Chinese of the sutras. Records of his talks show farmers, townspeople, women and men, monks and lay people coming to listen. He mostly skipped the old koan stories and talked about their actual lives: anger, worry, sleepiness, the neighbors. Third, how the unborn gets lost. Nobody is born angry. Something happens, you want your own way, and you turn the unborn mind into a fighting mind, which Bankei calls trading the Buddha-mind for something smaller. Don't fight the anger with more effort, he says. Just don't make it. Fourth, trust. Bankei was wary of teachers who told students to strain and grind for awakening. His advice is gentle: you already have it, so stop swapping it for something else. On an ordinary day, the unborn sounds like this: the kettle clicks off, and you just hear it. Someone cuts in line, and for one beat, before the story starts, there's only seeing.
screen: `THE BUDDHA-MIND IS UNBORN.` · `PLAIN WORDS FOR ORDINARY PEOPLE.` · `NOBODY IS BORN ANGRY.` · `YOU ALREADY HAVE IT.` · then, large: `STAY UNBORN.`

segments.voice: Sit however is comfortable and notice that seeing is already happening without your effort, and so is feeling: the seat, the air, the breath. When a thought starts building something, a plan, a complaint, a worry, notice the building and don't add the next brick. Come back to what's already working fine on its own; there's nothing to earn here.
The unborn. Bankei's word for the Buddha-mind everyone already has, never produced, so it never falls apart. Today's word.
Your line: the kettle clicks off. What's unborn needs no building. That's day one thousand three.

howItsDone: Zen students and teachers read Bankei's recorded talks and point to the unborn mind in everyday life; his way is often taught without koans, as trusting the mind that is already working.

chat.says: I've always had a short temper. Isn't that just how I was born?
options: Bankei would say no one is born angry: we make it on the spot, and can stop making it.
Bankei would say yes: temper is fixed at birth, so just accept it.
Bankei would say a bad temper proves you were born without any Buddha-mind at all.
chat.meaning: In Bankei's story the man can't show his temper on demand, so it isn't inborn: it's made when something sets it off.
